Press Release:


Water Restrictions
Hefty fines await consumers as municipalities implement water restrictions. Government lays the blame squarely on the drought, but water experts firmly believe it could have been prevented, despite low rainfall figures across the country. Carte Blanche asks: Is the drought perhaps a convenient scapegoat for mismanagement of resources and crumbling municipal infrastructure?


Script:



Promo's

10sec We all hope the drought will be broken in the next few months. But Gauteng's water restrictions might be here for the next ten years

15secs "Gauteng residents are complaining about the forced water restrictions, but it could get a lot worse.
Upsound Hilgard: We will throttle you until you get there
Water restrictions – who is to bless and who is to blame."

15secs "Could water restrictions have been avoided?
Upsound Anthony: I would venture to say...
How did we actually end up in the most serious water crisis we've ever had"

Insert script INSERT SCRIPT

V/o: This man is performing an action called throttling – a term which is set to become a household word over the next few years. He is busy cutting down, or throttling the water supply to an entire suburb, to prevent the city’s reservoirs from running dry…
"Link Derek
At a Joburg Water sign" The municipalities in gauteng are caught between a rock and a hard place. The national department of water and sanitation is the regulator of all our water. In gauteng, the municipalities, buy the water from them and sell it on to the public. And now the national department has decided to cut the amount of water they make available to the municipalities by 15%.
The new mayoral committee member dealing with water at the Joburg City council says they have no choice but to force us to reduce our consumption.
MMC But now they're going to give us less 15% actual volume, and unless we use 15% less volume on the other side of the reservoir, then we're going to run the reservoirs dry and then were going to be in big trouble
And since the restrictions have been introduced, we haven’t managed to save even half of the 15% - so, according to Joburg Water spokesperson Hilgard Matthews they have to literally turn off the taps
Hilgard We will throttle and we will take it down until we get our 15% from that area
And this gets many residents hot under the collar – why should residents suffer damage and discomfort when the municipality wastes so much water? During a quick runaround one morning this week, we saw numerous water leaks, not to mention raw sewerage running into our rivers... But the MMC says they are very close to the international standard in terms of wastage.
MMC We in joburg are above that norm, we're probably at about 17% water losses in the system. But the norm is between 12 and 15%. We'd like it to come down and we will get it to come down.
He says that the crisis is caused by the drought, and that the decision lies with the national department.
V/o: Gauteng's water comes from the Vaal river system. 60% of our economy and 45% of our population depend on the Vaal. Minister Mokonyane also says the Gauteng crisis is caused by the drought.
Minister "D:Is our very water security ar risk
M: Yes, our water security is highly at risk. If we have to actually go below 25% in terms of the volume of water in the Vaal dam we will actually find serious challenges of dealing with the future supply. Because it will impact negatively on the entire infrastructure of the system."
V/o: "With the Vaal Dam currently at 27% we are only 2% away from disaster.
And, while it is true that based on 110 years of rainfall records, 2015 was South Africa's driest year ever, water strategist Professor Anthony Turton says that we were always going to have a water crisis from 2015 onwards, even without a drought. One of the department’s own studies predicted this back in 2012. It also told the department how to prevent it. "
Anthony We'd known about this thing for a long period of time. And I draw your attention to a study that was done by the department of water affairs in 2012. In which they were looking at the whole vaal river system. And in 2012 they came up with the magic number of 15% reduction that had to be achieved to prevent the vaal river from running dry
"Link Derek
At a dam/water feature/park etc" The study came up with an 8point strategy that would enable us to avoid the crisis, one of which for the first time quoted the magical figure of cutting consumption by 15% - but this would only work if the other 7 were also implemented.
V/o: Anthony explains that the crisis has 2 main contributing factors – not enough clean water reaching the Vaal, and an extremely high salinity level in the water, caused by mine dump seepage and sewage flowing into the dam. And this is where things started going wrong.
Anthony So therefore you have to do one of two things if you're going to prevent that. You either have to reduce the salts from coming in in the first place, or you have to put more fresh water in the system to dilute it out. So given the fact that there was not yet desalination in place you now have to use the only clean water available, and that was guess what, from lesotho highlands water project.
V/o: The 2012 8-point plan offered a short term solution to avoid a crisis by 2016, a medium term solution to meet rising demands by 2020 and a more long term solution.
Anthony The immediate short term fix was to remove the salt coming into the system.
V/o: "Instead of having to waste good water on diluting the dam water’s high saline content, removing the salt before the water reaches the dam would not only save the clean Lesotho water, but would also add to the volume needed to meet the demand. But, four years after the study warned of the pending crisis if this was not done, the steps are still not entirely in place.
The medium term solution, to be able to meet the rising demand for water in the rapidly growing Gauteng province, was to bring the Lesotho Highlands Water Project Phase 2 online by 2020. If not, we simply will not have enough water by then. "
Anthony That means that the contracting had to take place 5 years before that, by 2015. The contract is still not fully in place as we sit here. So the delay in that system has meant it's not possible now, even if we don't have a drought, the first water that's going to flow is going to come in around 2025.
V/o: The minister must be aware of this study as she was premier of Gauteng in 2012, before she took charge of our national water affairs. However, she strongly denies that 2020 ever was the deadline.
Minister It was all along earmarked for 2025, but with anything possible we might actually make a breakthrough earlier than 2025, but remember its 2025
V/o: "According to Anthony, missing both the short and medium term deadlines has now compromised our water security for the next 10 years.
"
Anthony So, is the drought the cause of the crisis. I would venture to suggest that it's not.
And while the department is still running around trying to get all 8 points implemented, the shortage has hit us as predicted, and now they have no choice but to supply municipalities with less water. The municipalities are simply passing this on to the consumer, once again blaming it on the drought and not their own wastage.
MMC The situation I described to you about technical water losses or physical water losses, and revenue losses in the system are not new. The drought is new, you know. This drought is severe.
V/o: Infrastructure consultant Tian Claasens disagrees. The water system was designed to withstand the type of drought that only occurs once every 50 years. We are currently facing a less serious one in 20 year drought.
Tian The system has been overloaded significantly because of the wastage of water, because only about 50% of the water that is taken out of the system is eventually reticulated to consumers. Or, if it is reticulated to consumers there is no way we can measure it, and there is no way that we can control it.
V/o: By wastage, Tian means all water that’s unaccounted for – water that is not metered or paid for, like in some of our townships. .
MMC And you go right now and most of Soweto does not pay for water. And there are also people in the northern suburbs, i'm not picking on them only. There are all the informal settlements, which we will never try and individually meter. We have to do that as a human rights almost sort of issue. We have to supply them with water, it's not possible to take a water reticulation system in there and try to meter everyone.
But even if they have no choice but to supply free water to thousands of people, a lot is still lost through municipal leakages. The cause? The fact that since the late 1980's virtually no maintenance has been done. The international norm is to continually replace 2% of your infrastructure every year. Fortunately, about 3 years ago, Joburg Water realised the urgency of the looming crisis and started replacing infrastructure at a rate of 3.3 % per annum, almost double the international norm. But it will take a long time to wipe out the backlog built up over almost 30 years.
Hilgard So yes, we're ahead of the 2%, but the backlog is so big that we need to keep up this 3.3%, and if possibly, we need to keep this up for 8 to 10 years, and then we'd be able to then start saying that we're getting to a place where we know that the leaks are minimal throughout the system.
V/o: To their credit, in just 3 years of proper maintenance, they've already saved billions of litres.
Hilgard The same amount of water that we supplied to Soweto 10 years ago is the same quantity of water that we are supplying to Soweto now. This is despite the growth. Even within the city of johannesburg, in the last 3 financial years, and obviously the last one has been audited, but in the last three financial years we are using the same amount of water.
V/o: "As part of their turnaround, they've installed and are now successfully running one of the most efficient water management systems in the world. They can monitor water levels in every reservoir and tower in real time, and pick up faults on pumps as they happen. and much more. This makes reaction times much shorter which in itself saves millions of litres of water.
It also makes it easier to pinpoint the thirsty suburbs, guiding the decision on where and how to throttle water next. But, like the crisis facing the national department, the maintenance backlog will also only be wiped out by 2025, and they still haven't addressed the desalination issue.
So, three things seem clear - the drought is not the biggest issue in Gauteng , we have no choice but to change our behaviour to avert a catastrophe, and the research suggests that the crisis won't be over for at least ten years. Although the minister thinks otherwise."
Minister If we manage to save at least 15% of water we are providing, we can actually within a period of 6 moths, come back and review, but that does not mean we will be having our dams full. So the issue of 2025 as i'm saying will apply.... in fact we may even go beyond the 15% if we don't change our use of water. (Not accurate)
